Setting: We have transaction records of customers buying
CDs from a CD shop.

How do we categorize music?
• Each customer only likes a select few categories of music.

Idea:
• Represent a CD by the set of customers who bought it.
• Similar CDs have similar sets of customers, and vice-versa.

Example 1: Clustering Music CDs:
Collaborative Filtering

We can represent a CD as a point 𝑥𝑥1, 𝑥𝑥2, … , 𝑥𝑥𝑘𝑘∈{0,1}𝑘𝑘where
𝑥𝑥𝑖𝑖= 1 if and only if customer 𝑖𝑖bought the CD.

Clearly, 𝑘𝑘can be very big with major retailers or online
platforms.

Task: Find clusters of similar CDs.
• Similar CD’s have similar sets of customers, vice versa

Setting: We have a catalogue of academic research papers
in mathematics.

How do categorize the papers into fields of mathematics?
• Similar papers are likely to contain the same set of words.

We can represent a paper as a point 𝑥𝑥1, 𝑥𝑥2, … , 𝑥𝑥𝑘𝑘where
𝑥𝑥𝑖𝑖= 1 if and only if the word 𝑖𝑖appears in the document.

We may think of a document as a set of words or shingles
(last lecture).

• Vectors: Cosine similarity
• Sets: Jaccard similarity
• Points: Euclidean distance

The choice of similarity measure is very important and
requires domain knowledge.

Step 1: Pick a notion of cohesion of clusters.
Step 2: Merge clusters whose union is the most cohesive.

Cohesion could mean:
1. Diameter of a cluster = maximum distance between any
two points in the cluster.
2. Average distance between points in the cluster.
3. Density-based cohesion:
•
Take the number of points in the cluster divided by
some measure of volume


Volume could be diameter to the power of dimension of space
When do we stop merging clusters?

• If we fix the number of clusters beforehand, then it is a
trivial when to stop.

• Examples of other criteria:

Stop if diameter exceeds a threshold.

Stop if density is below some threshold.

Stop merging if resulting cluster is bad.

clustering algorithm.

• Identify some representatives of each cluster
• Assign each data point to a cluster by some rules

BFR [Bradley-Fayyad-Reina] is a variant of K-means
designed for large datasets that do not fit in main memory.

Assumption: Clusters are normally distributed around a
centroid in Euclidean space.
• Standard deviations may differ
across dimensions, but the
covariance is diagonal.


This means that clusters
are axis aligned.

Efficiency: This method requires memory in O(#clusters)
rather than O(#data).

Main idea: When we have high confidence that points
belong to a cluster, we can summarize and discard them
from RAM (main memory).

Each cluster can be summarized by:
• The number of points, 𝑵𝑵.
• The vector SUM = sum of points in the cluster.
• The vector SUMSQ, whose 𝑖𝑖𝑡𝑡𝑡component = sum of
squares of 𝑖𝑖𝑡𝑡𝑡coordinate of the points in the cluster.

A cluster.
All its points are
discarded from RAM

• Memory Savings: Each cluster is summarized using 2𝑑𝑑+ 1
values, rather than remembering all points in the cluster.

• The average in each dimension is SUM𝑖𝑖/𝑁𝑁.

SUM𝑖𝑖= 𝑖𝑖𝑡𝑡𝑡component of SUM.

•
Variance of a cluster has 𝑖𝑖𝑡𝑡𝑡component =

Note: Dropping the “axis-aligned” clusters assumption would require
storing full covariance matrix to summarize the cluster. So, instead of
SUMSQ being a d-dim vector, it would be a d x d matrix, which is too big!

Step 1: Initialize K clusters/centroids
Step 2: Load a small chunk of points from disk to memory
Step 3: For those points that have high probability of
belonging to one of the K clusters, we assign them
accordingly, then summarize and discard them.
Step 4: Run hierarchical clustering on the remaining points,
resulting in some extra mini-clusters, which are also
summarized
Step 5: Try to merge new mini-clusters from step 4 with
existing clusters
Repeat steps 2-5 until all points are examined.

Three classes of points to keep track of:
Discard set (DS) from Step 3
• Points close enough to one of the K centroids to be added
as a member of that cluster.
• They are thus summarized and discarded.
Compression set (CS) from Step 4
• Groups of points that are close to each other, but not
close to any existing centroid.
• These points are summarized as a minicluster, but not
assigned to one of the K big clusters.
Retained set (RS) from Step 4
• Isolated points (singleton clusters from step 4) that are
not summarized yet

Centroids

main memory.

• After the initial load of points, we apply one of the

the DS.
•

•
The points can then be discarded.

Step 4: Use an in-memory algorithm (e.g. hierarchical) to
cluster the remaining points and the old RS.
• Miniclusters go to the CS; isolated points go to the RS.

Step 5
The CS now has new members from step 4.  We can try to
merge the miniclusters in the CS if they are “close enough”.

If this is the final round, either:
• Merge a minicluster of CS or an isolated RS point to its
closest centroid
• Treat them as outliers (which are ignored)

•
So that it can be summarized and discarded.

Mahalanobis distance
Setting: A cluster is summarized by the parameters of a
Gaussian distribution with mean/centroid 𝑐𝑐= (𝑐𝑐1, … , 𝑐𝑐𝑑𝑑)
and standard deviation 𝜎𝜎= (𝜎𝜎1, … , 𝜎𝜎𝑑𝑑).
• Given a datapoint 𝑥𝑥= (𝑥𝑥1, … , 𝑥𝑥𝑑𝑑), the Mahalanobis distance
between the datapoint and the cluster is defined as:

• It is a normalized Euclidean distance from the centroid,
taking into account the standard deviations in each
dimension.


Lower Mahalanobis distance equates to higher
probability of belonging to that cluster.

How to decide whether a point is sufficiently close to a
cluster?
• Use the Mahalanobis distance as a threshold.

Choosing the threshold for
Mahalanobis distance (M.D.)

• If clusters are indeed normally distributed in 𝑑𝑑dimensions,
then one standard deviation = 𝒅𝒅.


68% of points will have M.D. <
𝑑𝑑.
• Take M.D. threshold to be
proportional to 𝑑𝑑.

When do we combine 2 CS miniclusters?
• Compute the variance of the combined subcluster.

𝑁𝑁, SUM, SUMSQ allow us to do this quickly.
•
Combine them if the combined variance
is below some threshold.

Issues with BFR:
• Assumes that clusters are
normally distributed and
axis-aligned.

CURE (Clustering Using Representatives)
• Assumes Euclidean space.
• Allows clusters to have any shape.
• Represent clusters using a collection
of representative points.
CURE is a two pass algorithm.

Pass 1:
0) Pick a random sample of points that fit in main
memory
1) Initial clusters:
•
Cluster these points hierarchically

E.g. merge clusters based on nearest pair of points
2) Pick representative points:
•
For each cluster, pick some representative points, as
dispersed as possible (like K-means initialization)
•
Move the representative points (say) 20% toward the
centroid of the cluster.

Pick (say) 4
remote points
for each
cluster.

After picking representative points, we discard all points of
the cluster, and only describe clusters using these
representatives.

Merge two clusters if they have a pair of representatives
sufficiently close.
• Describe resulting cluster by picking scattered
representatives out of the representatives of its parent
clusters, then shrink towards centroid again.
• We can keep merging until there are no more sufficiently
close clusters.

Pass 2:
Now, rescan the whole dataset and
visit each point p in the data set.

Place it in the “closest cluster”.
• Find the closest representative to p and
assign it to representative’s cluster.

• The boundary of large dispersed clusters will become
much smaller.
• Favours a small, dense cluster that is near a large,
dispersed cluster.

our clusters using metrics such as:
